articles.title: Meet Robert the robot looking after Vera, 74, in her own home
articles.summary: At least a thousand people across England use the droids, health tech company Cera says.
articles.body:
Vera Gadsdon, 74, is one of the residents at a retirement housing complex in Lewisham.

She has a carer, Pinar Elmaz, and a helper called Robert.

Robert reminds her when to take her medication, to do her washing and even gives her knitting tips.

Robert is a robot, just one of those that is now providing company and medical assistance in care homes. Some say the droids are cutting costs and freeing up staff.

But, having met Vera and Robert, I can't help wondering: if she could choose, would Vera prefer to speak to a robot or a relative?

Pinar says the droids, made by tech healthcare company Cera, are not a replacement for human carers but "another tool for us as well because we can always check in on them... make sure they've taken their medication and then make sure they've hydrated".

Hazelhurst Court has 24 residents with robots and they certainly seem to enjoy their new companions.

Each one contains their person's medical needs and individual calendar and is programmed to tell users when it's time to eat or play bingo or watch their favourite television show.

Some residents say the robots make them feel less lonely, while others say they use them to connect with their grandchildren.

These robots can clean, exercise - and care for you in old age. Would you trust them to?

During our visit, Robert is friendly, repeatedly asking Vera how she is and reassuring her "I'll be here if you need me".

"What would you enjoy chatting about today?" it asks.

But it does make mistakes when Vera wants to talk about knitting, often mishearing essential words and offering conversations on "biscuits and cakes" and "music, television, the garden or something else".

Tech expert James Erskine says when it comes to such robots, what needs to be considered is what they can do well and what they cannot.

"If a job can be followed to the letter like an instruction, a robot or computer can probably do it. If it needs problem-solving, judgement or emotional understanding, it needs a human," he says.

"AI is already helping surgeons during brain tumour operations, and driverless taxis being trialled on London's roads.

"In care, robots could be brilliant at monitoring health - vital signs, medication reminders, spotting falls. But can they really read someone's mental state, their happiness, their overall wellbeing?

"That depends on human connection, noticing the small things, knowing the person. So it's support, not substitute.

"The best outcome is tech taking on the routine tasks so carers have more time for the human side of care."

At least 1,000 people across England are using the robots, according to Cera.

Dr Ben Maruthappu, a former A&E doctor in London, is Cera's founder and chief executive. He says his personal experience of social care in the capital inspired him to look for solutions in tech.

"My mother had a fall and fractured her back and needed care at home so I needed to try and organise that care," he says. "What I thought would be a really simple process was actually excruciatingly difficult.

"I called lots of different home care agencies. We had this revolving door of carers looking after my mum, and I didn't even know their name - let alone how the care was going.

"How is it in this day and age, when I can get books and groceries delivered to my door at the click of a button, I have no idea the care my mum is receiving which is so much more important?"

He added he was motivated to build a better model of care where "technology addressed some of the issues and frictions in the care sector".

Now with 13,500 staff and almost £500m in annual revenue, Cera says it is Europe's largest health tech firm.

The company claims its AI tools reduce hospital admissions by up to 70% and its robots boost care teams' capacity by 20% and productivity by up to 80%.

Whether the needs being met include the human need for connection remains to be seen.

articles.title: October 2026 astrology: 5 Astrology and vastu tips to attract balance, clarity and positive energy
articles.summary: October 2026 is not necessarily a month to keep adding more. It may actually be a better month to look at what has already accumulated.
articles.body: October 2026 is not necessarily a month to keep adding more.It may actually be a better month to look at what has already accumulated. Money spent without thinking. Things lying unused around the house. Hundreds of screenshots on the phone. A work desk where yesterday's papers are still competing with today's priorities.Even our morning routine can become something we move through without consciously resetting ourselves.With October carrying a larger theme of review and reassessment, I would keep the remedies equally practical. You don't need to change your entire house or follow twenty complicated rituals.Start with these five things.Keep your wallet free from old bills and receiptsOpen your wallet today.You may find restaurant bills from three weeks ago, expired cards, old parking slips, random visiting cards and receipts you no longer remember keeping.Clear them.From a Vastu perspective, I prefer keeping the place associated with money clean and organised. But there is a practical financial lesson here too. While cleaning your wallet, look at what you have actually been spending on.Sometimes an old receipt tells you more about your money habits than a monthly budget does. Keep the cards and documents you genuinely need and remove the rest. Your wallet should carry your money, not your history.Review luxury spending before buying moreOctober is a particularly good month to distinguish between wanting something and wanting the feeling that comes with buying it.Before purchasing another watch, handbag, perfume, jewellery piece, gadget or expensive décor item, give yourself some time.Ask:Do I genuinely need this?Do I already own something similar?Would I still want it after 48 hours?There is nothing wrong with luxury. The problem begins when shopping becomes the quickest response to stress, boredom or the need for validation.This month, enjoy beautiful things. Just don't let every beautiful thing become yours.Keep the south-west of your home stable and clutter-freeTake a proper look at the South-West portion of your home.Has it slowly become the place where cartons, broken furniture, old luggage and things with no permanent location are dumped? In Vastu, I prefer keeping the South-West comparatively stable, organised and grounded. You don't necessarily need to place another remedy there.First remove what should not be there. Clean the area. Repair broken furniture. Organise what genuinely needs to remain.Sometimes the first Vastu remedy is not adding an object. It is removing five unnecessary ones.Declutter your phone and work deskWe understand physical clutter very easily. Digital clutter is less visible.Start with your phone. Delete duplicate photographs, unnecessary screenshots, unused apps and downloads you haven't opened in months. Organise important documents and back up what actually matters.Then move to your work desk. Remove dead pens, old coffee cups, tangled wires, outdated papers and things that have nothing to do with the work currently in front of you.Don't aim for an Instagram-perfect desk or an empty phone.The purpose is much simpler. When you need something, you should be able to find it without moving through fifty things you don't need.Add lemongrass aroma to your bathing routineMake your morning bath a small reset ritual this month. If lemongrass suits you, use a properly diluted lemongrass essential-oil preparation appropriate for bathing rather than adding concentrated essential oil directly to the skin or water.As you bathe, consciously use those few minutes to mentally separate yourself from yesterday's irritation, unfinished conversations and emotional baggage.Don't check your phone immediately before entering the shower and continue the same argument in your head while bathing.Let the bath mark a transition: Yesterday is over. articles.title: Doctors say radical plan to merge Scotland's health boards should be scrapped
articles.summary: BMA Scotland says there is no evidence that reducing the number of health boards from 14 to two will improve patient care.
articles.body:
Leading doctors are calling on the Scottish government to withdraw its plans to drastically reduce the number of health boards.

The new chairwoman of BMA Scotland, Dr Nora Murray-Cavanagh, said the proposal to cut the number from 14 to just two would be costly and time consuming - and that there was no clear evidence it would benefit patients.

First Minister John Swinney unveiled the plan a month ago , saying it would streamline management and free up resources for frontline care.

Health Secretary Angela Constance said she stood by the proposals and promised engagement with a range of groups including unions and NHS boards as the details were developed.

Swinney announced the plan as part of his Programme for Government at the start of September, describing it as the "most significant structural reform of our NHS in the devolution era".

Fourteen existing health boards would be reduced to just two Strategic Health Boards, covering the west and east of mainland Scotland, with different arrangements considered for the three island health boards.

Ministers said it would simplify administration and reduce duplication so that more resources could be directed to front line treatment as well as delivering more consistency in care across the country.

But members of the British Medical Association's Scottish Council raised serious concerns and voted to oppose the plan during a meeting on Wednesday.

After the vote, Murray-Cavanagh said it wanted the government to "withdraw and rethink its whole approach" and come up with a more immediate way of helping patients.

Swinney to cut number of health boards from 14 to two

Swinney suggests Scots will not travel further for health care under reforms

The GP from Wester Hailes in Edinburgh, who took up the role with BMA Scotland just a few weeks ago, stressed that doctors did not deny that the NHS needed to change.

She said: "Our position is not one that argues NHS reform isn't necessary – no-one thinks we can simply go on as we are.

"As doctors, we know better than most the precarious state of services across Scotland.

"But this is the wrong set of reforms, and it will set Scotland on a path of a costly, time consuming, resource-sapping reorganisation, with no serious engagement with those of us holding the service together and no clear evidence put forward on how it will benefit patients."

Murray-Cavanagh said members of the BMA's Scottish council had spoken passionately of their concerns about the impact the proposals would have on them and their patients.

She added: "At the core of everything is the lack of any evidence on how these reforms will practically make care better."

In response to the BMA's remarks, Health Secretary Angela Constance said the plans for NHS reform were focused on improving services for people across the country, regardless of where a person lives.

"They will simplify how people get the care they need and remove the current geographic and bureaucratic barriers that exist between 14 health boards, which we know are currently causing unwanted variation and duplication," she said.

She said the changes would build on work that was already under way, involving every NHS board in Scotland, to improve planning.

She added: "The development of detailed proposals will be supported by a full business case and will include engagement with NHS boards, staff representatives, trade unions, local government, integration authorities, social care partners and the public."

Analysis: Not the only group raising concerns

The BMA is the first medical organisation to publicly call on the government to rethink its plans.

The doctors' union is very much in favour of reform and for many years has issued stark warnings that without fundamental change, the NHS cannot survive.

But it has now come out strongly against the government's current plans to transform healthcare by reducing the number of regional health boards to two.

The first minister argued consolidation would reduce bureaucracy while freeing up more time and capacity to improve patient care. He also claimed it would reduce inequality for some patients.

They are also not alone in raising concerns that consolidation could actually widen health inequalities if people are forced to travel further for treatment. The patient safety commissioner, as well as some rural campaign groups, have echoed these fears.

The union also question where the evidence is that these reforms are in the interests of patients and NHS staff, saying a reorganisation could be time-consuming and costly.

Others have argued that structural reform does not address wider issues the NHS faces around access to social care, which the government is also trying to address.

It is also unclear whether this new structure will result in financial savings by cutting senior roles or streamlining departments.

At the moment, the NHS has a no compulsory redundancy programme which the government reiterated its commitment to after this announcement was made.

The union Unite, which represents thousands of health and social care workers in Scotland, warned ministers at the time that it was considering "all options" if the reorganisation results in cuts to jobs or frontline services.

articles.title: Mourners bury DR Congo official killed after defending Ebola response
articles.summary: Marie-Celestin Karondwa died of his injuries after being beaten at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot, on Sunday.
articles.body:
Mourners have gathered in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to bury a local politician who his party said was beaten to death after he defended the government’s Ebola response on the radio.

The funeral for Marie-Celestin Karondwa was held in the city of Butembo on Wednesday.

Karondwa was attacked on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in North Kivu province, according to his political party, the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDSP), which leads the DRC government. He died of his injuries at a local hospital.

“They beat him up and then set the house on fire,” his granddaughter, Sagesse Kavira, told The Associated Press news agency at the funeral.

The party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to the population”.

It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many were involved or what motivated it.

The killing follows a series of attacks on health workers and other responders as the Central African nation battles its 17th and deadliest Ebola outbreak, which has so far recorded more than 8,000 cases, including nearly 4,000 deaths.

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there is no vaccine or specific treatment, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Researchers are testing potential candidates, the agency said.

The WHO said Ebola was present in provinces including Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Sud Ubangi and Tshopo. It said Ituri remained the most affected.

Officials have tried to fight the outbreak through a village-based approach, but some residents have resisted, dismissing Ebola as a hoax amid deep distrust of the government.

Many believe the disease is a ruse for officials to siphon off money . Some refuse to report their symptoms due to disbelief or shame surrounding being an Ebola patient.

Responders say the scepticism has complicated their work, including in remote communities and newly emerging hotspots that are short of medical supplies and health workers.

The mistrust has been especially hard to overcome in rebel-held areas of eastern DRC, where decades of conflict and human rights abuses have left many residents wary of outsiders and state authorities.

Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s director general, has said the country’s east faces “a catastrophic collision of disease and conflict” hampering the response.

articles.title: Brit Awards boosted Manchester economy by £5m, study finds
articles.summary: Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig said the awards' move north for the first time was a "massive moment".
articles.body:
The Brit Awards' move to Manchester for the 2026 ceremony generated £5 million for the city and its surrounding area, research has found.

The annual awards ceremony, widely regarded as the UK's biggest night in music, was hosted in city for the first time this year after being held in the capital for its near 50-year history.

The move had a positive economic and social impact and created more than 3,000 temporary jobs, according to an independent study conducted by Amion Consulting.

Greater Manchester mayor Bev Craig praised the awards' move north as a "massive moment for our city region", with the 2027 event also set to be held in the city.

The show took place at Manchester's Co-op Live arena on 28 February in a ceremony hosted by comedian Jack Whitehall, and featuring performances from stars including Harry Styles, Olivia Dean, Raye and Mark Ronson.

It generated £5m in net additional expenditure in Manchester, with £3.6m coming from visitors and £1.4m as a result of organiser and partner expenditure.

Craig said the decision to hold the event in Manchester "was a recognition not only of our unmatched music heritage, but our growing reputation for putting on national and global events and making a success of them".

She said such events brought millions of pounds into Manchester's economy, boosting the culture and hospitality industries and created opportunities for people.

"We've done it once in style, and we'll do it again next year," she said, adding she was excited to help make 2027 an even bigger year for the Brits.

Manchester City Council leader Garry Bridges said this year's award show was "phenomenally successful".

"The partnership between the Brits and Manchester went so much further – with a massive social and economic reach right across the city and into our communities, which is still being felt now," he added.

The study also found the event generated £3.45m in gross value added and created 3,099 one-week temporary jobs for Manchester-based workers, equivalent to 15,497 days of employment.

It also found that 92% of award show attendees rated the experience as excellent or good, with the move to Manchester helping to engage new audiences in the Brits themselves and in wider events surrounding the ceremony.

The study found that audience feedback on the event was "overwhelmingly positive", while media and digital coverage helped to amplify Manchester's profile on a global stage.

It also spawned a number of events centred around the Brits, with community-focused initiatives, educational engagement, networking events and other programmes held in Manchester in the weeks leading up to the ceremony.

The study found that the social impact of the event could be monetised at £11.2m, taking into account factors such as cultural participation, digital engagement and Manchester's strengthened profile as an events destination.

articles.title: Poll scopes interest in car ferry between Guernsey and Jersey
articles.summary: There is currently one weekly vehicle service between Guernsey and Jersey run by Brittany Ferries.
articles.body:
Islanders are being polled on their level of interest in a regular vehicle ferry service to run between Jersey and Guernsey.

Islands Unlimited began its foot passenger sailings between the islands in 2025.

There is currently only one sailing for cars a week between the islands - on a Wednesday - and run by Brittany Ferries.

Islands Unlimited said it was currently just an "idea", while nothing had yet been decided on whether a car service would come to fruition.

In an email to customers, Islands Unlimited said it was "looking at" whether to run a vehicle ferry "three to four days a week".

It added: "Before going any further we want to understand whether islanders would actually use it, how often, and what would make it worthwhile."

​The online poll asks residents if they would welcome a more regular service, whether their preference would be for it to operate seasonally and how frequently they might use it, and for what purpose.

They are also being canvassed on cost, with options ranging from £60 to £140 for a car and one passenger.

The firm took the "difficult decision" in September to end its foot sailings early after problems with its only ship's starboard main engine.

The daily service between Guernsey and Jersey, with weekend sailings to Alderney, had been due to run until Sunday 18 October.

Islands Unlimited has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: We're still cold at £300 a month' - Redditch residents fear energy price rise
articles.summary: Redditch residents say they are worried they will not be able to afford heating.
articles.body:
A pensioner says trying to keep warm and afford heating this winter will be "horrific" amid rising energy costs.

Pat Snell, from Redditch, Worcestershire, said she and her husband, John, who had a stroke, relied heavily on heating to keep him comfortable last winter.

"Even on a fixed-price tariff, our energy bills were £300 a month, and we were still cold," she said.

Snell raised concerns about further rises as millions of households in England, Scotland and Wales face higher energy bills from Thursday , when Ofgem's latest energy price cap increase comes into force. The regulator said typical households on standard variable tariffs will pay about £60 more a year, taking annual bills to £1,723.

The extra cost comes at a time when, Snell said, her household was already carefully managing energy use.

"We never even put the temperature up over 18C, and most of the rooms were closed.

"I don't even want to think about what it's going to cost in December, January and February."

Snell added that her fixed-rate tariff comes to an end in late October, meaning they could soon face higher costs.

The government said households would see some relief through its removal of VAT on domestic electricity bills, which it said had helped limit the increase, while the Warm Home Discount will provide eligible households with £150 off their bills this winter.

Snell is not the only resident in the town that is concerned about struggling to afford heating and other essentials this winter.

Another pensioner, Lorraine Stevenson, said she was already limiting energy use where possible.

"I live on my own, and I live in a small house, so I struggle because obviously, just on a pension, it's not easy," she said. "Any reduction helps.

"I look forward to getting the winter fuel payment. People say it doesn't really help, but it does help through the winter months because obviously you're paying a lot more."

She added: "You don't keep the house really warm, but you can't be cold, can you? Especially as the older you get."

Among others worried about the rise is Najibullah Rahimi, who came to the UK from Afghanistan with his family about a year ago.

He told the BBC he is currently seeking work and is expecting his benefits to be capped, leaving him concerned about how his family will manage as household costs continue to rise.

"The gas bill and electricity bill and internet bills and money for the children are difficult now for me," he said.

The additional pressure of higher winter energy bills, he said, would make an already difficult situation even more challenging.

Kelly Birkett, an accountant from Redditch, works from home. She is a mother of two and her husband is self-employed.

While they are both earning, the cost of energy is continuing to place pressure on the household income, and they are reining in family experiences.

"It's heartbreaking how much money you don't have to actually live your life - not just survive, but to live it and have those memories with your family and your friends and your children.

"As a family we work really hard and we wonder why? I don't think the politicians 'get it' and because they don't get it, they think they're doing enough but they're not."

The rise affects around 22 million households on default tariffs regulated by Ofgem, while about 11 million households on fixed-rate deals will not see their prices change immediately.

A typical household on a standard variable tariff will see annual bills rise by about £60 to £1,723, although the amount paid will ultimately depend on how much energy is used.

Ofgem said the increase had been driven largely by higher wholesale gas prices linked to conflict in the Middle East. The regulator said prices remain around 52% lower than they were at the height of the energy crisis in 2022, although charities and consumer groups have warned many households are still struggling with costs that remain well above pre-crisis levels.

The government said its removal of VAT on domestic electricity bills had helped limit the increase, with Ofgem estimating bills would otherwise have been about £45 higher. Eligible households can also receive a £150 Warm Home Discount this winter.

For many of those the BBC spoke to in Redditch, the concern was not just about a £5-a-month increase, but what it means when colder weather arrives and household budgets are already stretched.

"We'll just have to cut down on something else," said Stevenson.

Caroline Fortune, from energy advice charity Act on Energy, said many households had not yet felt the full effect of recent energy price increases because energy use typically falls during the summer months.

"The price cap went up in July, and because we haven't all turned our heating on yet, we've not felt it yet," she said.

"On 1 October it's due to go up again, and it's predicted to go up again in January, so it's something we need to be aware of."

Fortune said consumers should regularly review their tariff and not assume staying with the same supplier would offer the best value.

She encouraged households to check whether they were eligible for support schemes, including the Warm Home Discount, and to seek advice early if they feared falling behind on payments.

As temperatures fall, she advised people to be mindful of their energy use and focus heating on the rooms they spend most time in.

"If you're really struggling, heat the person, not the room," she said.

She said demand for help from the charity had risen as households grappled with multiple financial pressures.

"It's not as simple as having one small problem," she said.

"People's lives have got more complicated."

articles.title: Fuel prices leave people in the South asking 'what can we do?'
articles.summary: Record fuel prices across the country have left people in the South looking for ways to cope.
articles.body:
Record fuel prices across the country have left people in the south of England looking for ways to cope with the rising costs.

Earlier this week, the RAC said diesel prices in the UK had reached an all time high , with the cost of petrol also rising, due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

One garage manager from Berkshire said he had noticed a change in customer behaviour, with customers more likely to put £20 of fuel in, rather than fill their tanks up.

Meanwhile, a small charity helping people with multiple sclerosis (MS) in Dorset said it would have to find ways to cut costs, as it was now costing an extra £2,000 a year to run a key minibus service.

The MS Centre Dorset runs a fleet of five minibuses, helping users across the county to get to its base in West Parley.

But manager Diana Logan‑Watts said diesel prices had "rocketed so quickly" that the extra costs were "not something that we had budgeted into account".

On Monday, the RAC said diesel prices had entered "uncharted territory" and served as a reminder of "just how exposed the UK is to events occurring far away".

It said diesel prices had hit an all-time high of 199.33p per litre - rising by just under 40% since the US-Israel conflict with Iran erupted at the end of February.

Logan-Watts said this the MS Centre Dorset would "keep on keeping on" despite the vast cost increases, and ensure users could still get to the centre.

"But these rising costs have a knock-on effect, and we don't want to put additional prices and costs onto our members who are already struggling with the cost of living," she said.

"So we have to try and absorb those costs elsewhere, and one of those ways is thinking more closely about the additional services that we're able to offer, like trips.

"These make a real positive difference to our members lives, but will have to be looked at in more depth and ask where the money's going to come from."

It's not just charities in the South feeling the pinch though, with Southampton taxi driver Neil McLean asking "what can we do?" about the soaring costs.

"We've got to earn a living, and none of us are happy," he said.

"It's not putting money in our pockets, it's taking money out of our pockets - and it needs to stop."

David Price owns Southampton-based DCP Haulage, and said if things did not improve he would have to look at "parking up trucks" or "actually downscaling".

"We just can't physically afford the fuel prices, we're looking an extra £250 a week per vehicle," Price said.

"We have downscaled a lot lately and we have talked about packing it all up.

"It's not worth it with these prices - you're just not making any money."

Ian Govier manages the Littlewick Green Motor Company garage in Maidenhead, and said his costs had "gone up dramatically over the years".

"Ten years ago, we'd look at having [a profit margin of] 6p a litre, now I really need close to 15p a litre to still have the same profit," he said.

He said he had also spotted customers habits changing, including more using cash as a way to "control their budgets".

"We are definitely seeing instead of putting your normal £50 pounds in to fill up, a lot of people are now sticking in £10, £20," he said.

Amid the increase in costs, Govier said he was also having to tackle thefts - with some using illegal "ghost" registrations to prevent cameras from reading their number plates.

He said he had been forced to invest in a new camera system to tackle such thefts, which also "eats into profits".

"If you don't have a profit you can't invest in the cameras, you can't invest in your staff, you can't invest in people," he added.

Speaking at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool on Monday, the Chancellor said the time for the government to deal with questions around rising fuel costs would be the Budget - near the end of October.

John Healey told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I'm acutely concerned and conscious about how hard it is for families. I see that at the pumps myself.

"We can't remove the cost of living pressures, we can't remove the prices that people are having to pay, but where we can we will act and we will give people just a bit of breathing space, and the same goes for the cost to business."

articles.title: 'Posting on TikTok helped me through a dark time'
articles.summary: Josie North is co-founder of Regrettable Games, and posts on TikTok about struggling with her skin.
articles.body:
When Josie North and her brother, Harry, created their own party game inspired by a house fire in their family home, it looked like the only way was up.

The pair founded Hot House Games and co-created "Hit Send", a game that challenges players to send risky or funny texts for points, with YouTube collective the Sidemen .

After the game failed to sell as many units as they had hoped upon its launch, the siblings, from Bridgnorth, were determined to create better products, but their plans were hit by a setback.

North had been experiencing rash-like flare-ups on her skin since 2021. Despite treatment with steroid creams, the condition spread across her body and caused debilitating pain.

"From there, my life was never the same again... and this is the first time, this summer, looking in the mirror, that I recognise this person again," said North, who has spoken about her journey on TikTok.

"I've been in and out of hospital, A&E, looked quite literally like something of a horror movie, many a time."

She said it meant that her brother had to do a lot of "heavy lifting" with the business during times when she could not physically work.

"I came off an immunosuppressant early last year... and I had to go into hospital... I could hardly walk; my parents had to hold me up."

"They had to feed me with a teaspoon because I couldn't even open my mouth wide enough to properly eat; I was just in horrific, horrific pain."

Still working with the Sidemen - six influencers who have more than 23 million subscribers on the video platform - they began to create three new games and rebranded as Regrettable Games.

"My brother actually has a degree in psychology... he is very good at coming up with the game's mechanics, which is essentially how the game plays; how it works psychologically," she said.

"Where my expertise comes into play is the branding side and the packaging behind it... I think having that is almost as important as the actual game itself."

While dealing with flare-ups and trying to keep the business running, North took to social media to post about her skin.

"I felt like it just completely almost disfigured my face in a way," she said.

"I remember thinking to myself, 'I just feel embarrassed about the fact that people will look at me and probably think, 'Oh gosh, she's gone downhill; what's happened to her?'

"So I thought I'm actually going to be really open about it online and reach as many people as I possibly can."

North posted some of her worst flare-ups on TikTok. "When I started talking about it, some of my videos started going viral," she said.

"Throughout my journey, the community that I met on TikTok has been something that has literally carried me through at times.

"Being able to talk to people who are going through exactly the same thing when you literally sometimes do feel like you're the only person in the world that could be going through that much pain... having those people there, it's been amazing."

She said she wanted to help others who were going through similar struggles to her.

"At least there's been a little ray of sunshine in such a dark, dark period," she added.

The pair now have three party games on sale and will release four more next year.

"The main hope is that all the games do well across the world, and then we keep bringing out more and more games with different innovative twists, and bringing excitement to people's worlds," she said.

"I'd love to be able to carry on helping people with conditions such as mine and help people understand that beauty isn't just skin deep."

She said she has always pushed herself to never give up.

"Sometimes I couldn't even work, but I would try my best to at least get out of the house with my mum to go for a coffee just so I could see a glimpse of positivity in each day," she said.

"I remember a lot of people would comment on my TikTok saying, 'How do you even leave the house like that?'

"It would have been so easy just to give up and lie in bed... but I've always kind of been like, 'No, you need to carry on even at your hardest times'."

articles.title: 'A thrill' to find unknown Iris Murdoch artwork in Oxford attic
articles.summary: An expert on the author describes discovering 80 unknown works by the writer in Oxford.
articles.body:
Miles Leeson has been studying Dame Iris Murdoch - one of Britain's best-loved authors - for more than a decade.

So when he got a call last year alerting him to the possible discovery of new work by the writer, he did not get his hopes up straight away.

But, climbing into a dusty Oxford attic, he was gobsmacked to find a treasure trove of art created by the Booker-Prize-winning novelist.

Almost 80 paintings and sketches, which had laid undisturbed in the eaves for decades, are now on display for the first time at the centre Leeson runs in West Sussex.

Dame Iris lived in the house in the early 1940s, after arriving at university in Oxford in her early 20s.

"Going into that house really did feel like stepping back in time," Leeson said.

"A space that hadn't really been explored for a number of years, dusty, cobwebs - it really did feel like a complete treat to be invited in.

"To find the actual materials that we didn't know existed - what a thrill. I brushed off the dust but other than that they are as they were found."

The highlight of the exhibition is the author's only known self-portrait, which Leeson said was his favourite piece.

"It shows us Murdoch in a new light. There is a frisson when you come and have a look," he said.

Other pieces were inspired by surrealist artists she admired, like Paul Nash and Salvador Dali, while the building threat of war in Europe also influenced her paintings.

The free exhibition will run until December at the University of Chichester's library, and afterwards there are hopes the art may return to Oxford or a national museum.

articles.title: Employee faked sick leave for a Coorg trip, then manager sent the viral reel with five awkward words
articles.summary: A sick day can sometimes become the most complicated day off, especially when social media decides to join the story.
articles.body: A sick day can sometimes become the most complicated day off, especially when social media decides to join the story.A Reddit user on r/antiLinkedIn shared how a planned Friday trip to Coorg turned into an awkward workplace episode. The employee claimed to have stomach flu while actually heading out for a holiday. The plan might have worked, except a holiday reel accidentally put the employee in the frame.The sick leave excuse had one small problemAccording to the Reddit post, the employee took Friday off to travel to Coorg and told the manager that they had stomach flu.There was no mention of the trip to the workplace. Instead, the employee went to a homestay and apparently ended up appearing in the background of a video featuring people dancing.The unexpected part came later. The video reportedly took off on Instagram and crossed 13,000 likes.That made a private holiday much less private.Monday brought an awkward messageWhen the employee returned to work on Monday, the situation apparently became clear.The Reddit user said their skip-level manager sent them the reel and wrote: “Hope your stomach is better.”It was a short message, but the meaning was difficult to miss.The employee said they were still employed after the incident, but claimed that their subsequent WFH requests were no longer being approved because the manager had lost trust in them.The internet found the story painfully familiarThe post quickly attracted amused reactions from other Reddit users. Some laughed at the timing, while others pointed out the obvious risk of using a false excuse when social media can expose plans unexpectedly.One commenter summed up the lesson bluntly: “Lies are short lived.”Another joked about deleting Instagram altogether.The original poster also appeared surprised by how quickly the story travelled, replying that they had not expected the reel to go viral.A holiday can stay private, but a viral reel cannotThe interesting part of this story is not really the Coorg trip. Taking a day off is normal. The trouble came from giving a reason that did not match what happened.A holiday photo shared with friends can remain buried in someone's feed. A reel that suddenly reaches thousands of people is a different matter.And once a workplace connection sees it, explaining the coincidence can become harder than simply asking for a day off.Social media has changed the old workplace ruleEarlier, an excuse given to a manager usually stayed between a few people. Today, a single tagged post can travel far beyond its original audience.This Reddit story is a humorous example, not evidence that every workplace handles leave or WFH in the same way. Still, it captures an increasingly familiar workplace reality: online posts can sometimes reveal more than their creators intended.Disclaimer: This article is based on a Reddit post and comments shared by users. articles.title: Gujarat man who reported grandmother-in-law’s murder confesses to killing her, 2 others in 2022
articles.summary: AHMEDABAD: A man who informed police about the alleged murder of his grandmother-in-law in Gujarat’s Surat district was himself involved in the killing
articles.body: AHMEDABAD: A man who informed police about the alleged murder of his grandmother-in-law in Gujarat’s Surat district was himself involved in the killing and two other murders in 2022, allegedly with the intention of grabbing property, police said.Accused Madhavdas Sadhu had initially told police that his grandmother-in-law, Shantaben Vasava, a resident of Kosamba, had allegedly been murdered four to five years ago by his wife Urmila and her cousin Afzal. He claimed her body had been buried under concrete inside a house.Acting on the information, Crime Branch officials took Afzal into custody and questioned him. Afzal denied having any knowledge about Shantaben’s murder, according to a police release issued on Wednesday.The case took a turn when police questioned Madhavdas in Afzal’s presence.Madhavdas then told police that he had falsely implicated Afzal as he feared that his wife, who had left home around nine months ago with their son and allegedly taken valuables, and Afzal could implicate him in a case, police said.He subsequently confessed to killing Shantaben along with his wife Urmila, the release said.“Madhavdas said that on the night of October 7, 2022, he and Urmila killed his grandmother-in-law Shantaben Vasava with a pillow while she was sleeping. They put her body in a drum, poured three bags of cement mixed with water over it, closed the drum and kept it inside the house,” the release said.Around three-and-a-half months later, the couple allegedly cut open the drum and buried the body along with the cement in a pit dug in the verandah of the house, it said.Police said Madhavdas gave relatives different accounts of Shantaben’s death. He allegedly told his wife’s relatives that she had died of Covid-19 in Valthara, while telling his own relatives that she had died in Kosamba.According to police, the alleged murder was committed with the intention of taking possession of Shantaben’s property.In another alleged murder, Madhavdas and Urmila allegedly killed his 65-year-old mother in 2022.“Manjulaben Sadhu, mother of Madhavdas Sadhu, had suffered paralysis around 2021, and she was bedridden with sores on parts of her body. The couple allegedly strangled her with a pillow and told relatives and villagers that she had died due to paralysis. Her cremation was subsequently carried out at the Chakli Talav crematorium in Dholka,” the release said.The third alleged victim was Madhavdas’ sister-in-law Bharti, alias Bhagwati, who was married to Kamlesh Vasava and was living with Shantaben at Kosamba.“His brother-in-law Kamlesh allegedly died by suicide in his native village, and Bharti continued to live with his grandmother Shantaben. She later developed severe tuberculosis,” the release said.On the night of February 25, 2022, the couple allegedly strangled Bharti with a pillow and later claimed that she had died due to tuberculosis. Her last rites were performed with burial at Kosamba, it said.It was not immediately clear whether Urmila had been taken into custody.Legal proceedings are being initiated against the accused in the matter, and further investigation is underway, police said.(With Agency Inputs)You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Ahmedabad | Silver Rate in Ahmedabad | Bank Holidays in Ahmedabad | Public Holidays in Ahmedabad | Ahmedabad AQI | Weather in Ahmedabad | Petrol Price in Ahmedabad | Diesel Price in Ahmedabad | CNG Price in Ahmedabad | LPG Price in AhmedabadStay updated with the latest Ahmedabad news.
